source_read: PDF (version of record, born-digital), J Psychopharmacol 20(2): 188-193, all pages (text, reference list); text extracted with pdftotext and every number in the claim checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi (pp. 188-191)

claims.overstatement: Three small wording points. (1) 'earlier studies often did not record other drugs': the review says some of the earlier investigations did not capture data on other drugs (p. 191). Use 'some', not 'often'. (2) 'Studies that compared people who use ecstasy with people who use no drugs therefore cannot separate ecstasy from the other drugs': the review says it is difficult to draw conclusions on MDMA from studies with non-user controls (p. 189). 'Cannot' is a little stronger than the source; 'can hardly' or 'have difficulty separating' would match. (3) 'up to 234 people who used ecstasy': the source phrase (samples of up to 234 polydrug ecstasy users and polydrug controls who did not use ecstasy, p. 189) can also be read as up to 234 people in total, ecstasy users plus controls. The review does not say which, and the primary studies were not read. The claim correctly says the figures are second-hand and unappraised; this is a brief narrative overview with no methods section.
claims.note: All numbers checked on p. 189: 90-100% (three earlier studies: Schuster et al., 1998; Rodgers, 2000; Winstock et al., 2001; time frame of 'co-use' not stated), 1-9 pills cumulative, all novices had smoked cannabis at least once in the preceding month and 32% on five or more occasions (Scholey et al., 2004, a web-based survey according to the title in the reference list, sample size not given in the review), up to 234. The cannabis and ecstasy literature is described as inconsistent (p. 190). Several of the studies cited for cannabis explaining the psychopathology are the authors' own (Daumann et al., 2001, 2004). The abstract is firmer than the body: it says cannabis was shown to contribute to psychological problems and cognitive failures in people who use ecstasy, while p. 190 calls that literature inconsistent; the claim follows the body. No funding or conflict-of-interest statement is printed.

anchors.extracted: A brief overview of polydrug use as a confound in research on ecstasy/MDMA: the most commonly co-used substances are alcohol, cannabis and stimulants (amphetamines and cocaine); the most consistent finding cited is subtle memory deficits with heavy ecstasy use, and polydrug use is called one of the most serious confounds.

The overwhelming majority of people who use ecstasy also take other psychoactive drugs, most commonly alcohol, cannabis and stimulants (three studies cited), so conclusions about MDMA from studies with non-user controls are difficult. In recent studies with samples of up to 234 polydrug ecstasy users and polydrug controls not using ecstasy, raised psychopathology went with polydrug use in general, not ecstasy specifically (Parrott et al., 2001; Thomasius et al., 2003; Roiser & Sahakian, 2004). Such controls mostly used drugs more moderately than the ecstasy groups (nine studies cited).

anchors.locator: Cannabis: psychopathological sequelae and cognitive deficits..., 1st paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Most people who use MDMA used cannabis before starting ecstasy and continue alongside it. In one recent survey (Scholey et al., 2004) every novice (cumulative 1-9 pills) had smoked cannabis at least once in the preceding month and 32% on five or more occasions; the more pills taken, the more frequent the prior cannabis use. Earlier studies found 90-100% co-use of cannabis (Schuster et al., 1998; Rodgers, 2000; Winstock et al., 2001).

anchors.locator: Cannabis section, left column 3rd paragraph to right column 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The literature on cannabis's contribution is inconsistent. Self-reported psychopathology was mainly tied to cannabis in Daumann et al. (2001; 28 combined, 28 cannabis-only, 28 non-users), Morgan et al. (2002) and Daumann et al. (2004; 60 abstinent polydrug ecstasy users and 30 controls, 38 re-examined after 18 months). Other groups tied it to ecstasy and not cannabis, or found fewer complaints with cannabis co-use (Milani et al., 2002; Parrott et al., 2002). On cognition, most studies tied deficits to MDMA, some found an added cannabis effect, a minority found cannabis more closely linked; one amphetamine study and a small fMRI pilot (8 people using MDMA only) pointed to cannabis offsetting effects.

anchors.locator: Summary and perspectives for future research, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Findings in people who use MDMA may partly reflect pre-existing traits, drug use in general or lifestyle; polydrug use is one of the most important confounds; some of the earlier investigations did not capture data on other drugs, and many used poorly matched controls (non-users, or people using other drugs more moderately).

anchors.locator: Summary and perspectives for future research, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Cross-sectional designs will never be perfect and longitudinal ones may not suffice; the authors propose prospective designs: large cohorts of young people not (yet) using drugs but in risk groups, followed and re-examined over years, with drug histories recorded and psychological and cognitive testing; plus animal studies of drug interactions.

Narrative overview without methods: no search strategy, selection criteria or appraisal of the cited studies; all prevalence and sample figures are taken from cited studies, several of them the authors' own.

key_findings.correction: Content and location confirmed, but the source is hedged: it says it is difficult to draw conclusions on MDMA from studies with non-user controls (p. 189), not that such comparisons cannot isolate its effects. Suggested: '...so comparisons with people who use no drugs make it difficult to draw conclusions about MDMA's effects.'
Keeps the source's ambiguous wording correctly: 'up to 234' may count the ecstasy groups or the whole samples.

Could add that Scholey et al. (2004) is a web-based survey (its title in the reference list, p. 192), so the novice figures come from a self-selected online sample whose size the review does not give.
Gonzalez et al. (2004) is titled as a methamphetamine study in the reference list (p. 191): confirmed.

The source says some of the earlier investigations did not capture data on other drugs (p. 191, Summary 1st paragraph), not that earlier studies often did not. Replace 'often' with 'some earlier studies'. The rest is confirmed.

reporting_issues.note: Reference titles checked: Volkow et al. 2001b and Voytek et al. 2005 (p. 193) and Gonzalez et al. 2004 (p. 191) all say methamphetamine; the text says amphetamine users (pp. 189-190). The mapping to project ids was not checked (outside this source).

Within this source: the sentence (p. 189) does present the result as associations in the 15 users, so a reading as a comparison with controls is possible but not forced ('poorer performance' invites it). The point that the primary study did not compare test scores with controls rests on the project's card for that study, which I did not check.

Text p. 189 'Renemann et al., 2002'; reference list p. 192 'Reneman ... (2002) Use of amphetamine by recreational users of ecstasy (MDMA) is associated with reduced striatal dopamine transporter densities'; findings not described in the text.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high (no systematic search); domain judgments reasonable.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the abstract's causal wording ('shown to contribute') against the body's 'inconsistent' (p. 190) is the main gap, and the card records it.

missed: The two wording slips above (KF0 'cannot isolate', KF10 'often') also appear in claim cl_gen_polydrug; correcting the card will help the claim follow the source's hedged wording.
